title: Transitions
lead: Transition questions give you a short text with a blank and ask “Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?” The four choices are transition words or phrases. These questions test how well you understand the text at least as much as they test the words: you cannot pick the connector until you know how the two ideas relate. They are fast points once you know the system, because every transition belongs to a small set of categories.

parts.title: Part 1 · The core idea
parts.html:
A transition is a logic signpost. It tells the reader how the next idea relates to the one before. Every relationship goes in one of three directions, and inside each direction a transition has a more exact job.

DirectionJobIn plain wordsTransitions
Continuation
the second idea keeps going the same way		Addition“and another point”additionally, also, furthermore, moreover, in addition
Similarity“this works the same way”similarly, likewise, in the same way
Example“here is a specific case”for example, for instance, specifically
Emphasis“and this is even stronger”indeed, in fact, notably
Clarification“to say it another way”in other words, that is
Sequence“before, during or after”first, next, then, subsequently, finally, meanwhile, previously
Contrast
the second idea turns		Direct contrast“the opposite is true here”however, by contrast, in contrast, conversely, on the other hand
Concession“true, and yet”nevertheless, nonetheless, still, even so, though
Replacement“not that, this”instead, rather
Cause and effect
one idea explains the other		Result“so this followed”therefore, thus, consequently, accordingly, hence, as a result, for this reason
Reason“this is why”because, since, given that

Five of these jobs in a sentence:

Addition. The city widened its bicycle lanes last spring. Furthermore, it installed two hundred new bike racks.
Example. Many birds use tools to reach food. Some crows, for instance, bend twigs into hooks.
Concession. The bridge is more than a century old. Nevertheless, it carries thousands of cars every day.
Result. Heavy rain flooded the main road. Consequently, the race was moved to the following week.
Sequence. The play opened in a small theater in 1998. Previously, three producers had turned it down.

The whole question reduces to one thing: what is the logical relationship between the two ideas? Decide that from their meaning. Then pick the direction, then the job, then the word. Logic comes first and vocabulary second.

parts.title: Part 2 · The method
parts.html:
1. Read the idea before the blank and the idea after it. Do not skim, and do not read only the sentence with the blank. The relationship usually depends on the sentence before.
  2. Summarize each idea in a few words. “The plan was costly” and “the council approved it” become costly and approved anyway. The “anyway” in your own summary already shows the contrast. If the text is hard, turn each sentence into a short bullet point.
  3. Label the direction before thinking of a word. Say “contrast”, “continuation” or “cause and effect”. Predicting the category first protects you from a choice that sounds right but signals the wrong relationship.
  4. Test the exact job. Usually only one choice is from the right direction. If two are, ask what the second idea does: add, illustrate or emphasize? Oppose, concede or replace?
  5. Plug it in and reread. Read both ideas with your choice in place. If the signpost contradicts what the text does, the choice is wrong.

When two choices are from the same family, the difference is in how each is used:

Contrast wordUse
howeverGeneral contrast
nevertheless, nonetheless, still“Despite that”: side 2 happens in spite of side 1
in contrast, by contrastTwo different things compared side by side
insteadOne thing replaces another
Example. The museum's attendance declined sharply after 2008. ______ the museum's revenue rose, because ticket prices increased. Declined vs. rose → opposite directions → contrast → However, / Nevertheless,

parts.title: Part 3 · Worked example
parts.html:
Iraqi artist Nazik Al-Malaika, celebrated as the first Arabic poet to write in free verse, didn’t reject traditional forms entirely; her poem “Elegy for a Woman of No Importance” consists of two ten-line stanzas and a standard number of syllables. Even in this superficially traditional work, ______ Al-Malaika was breaking new ground by memorializing an anonymous woman rather than a famous man. A) in fact,
B) though,
C) therefore,
D) moreover,

Summaries. Before: she still used traditional forms. After: even there, she did something new.

Direction. Traditional against new: the second idea turns. Contrast.

ChoiceDirectionVerdict
A) in fact,Continuation (emphasis)Would strengthen “traditional”. The sentence goes the other way.
B) though,ContrastCorrect. The only contrast word.
C) therefore,Cause and effectUsing a traditional form did not cause her to break new ground.
D) moreover,Continuation (addition)Would add another point in the same direction.

You might have predicted “however”. It is not offered, and “though” does the same job.

parts.title: Part 4 · Cause and effect has a direction
parts.html:
Cause-and-effect words point one way or the other. A result word comes after the cause and introduces what followed. A reason word introduces the cause itself.

The gardeners watered the seedlings twice a day. As a result, the seedlings grew quickly. cause first → result word → effect The seedlings grew quickly because the gardeners watered them twice a day. effect first → reason word → cause

Do not invent a cause. Two facts about the same subject are not automatically cause and effect, and one event happening after another does not prove the first caused the second. “The streets were wet. Leila carried an umbrella.” These may be connected, but the text has not said that one caused the other. Use a cause-and-effect word only when the passage itself gives the link.

parts.title: Part 5 · The traps
parts.html:
Trap 1: contrast that is really a consequence.

The program was expensive; ______ it attracted few participants.

A contrast word sounds sophisticated here, but few participants is what you would expect from a high price. Side 2 goes the same way as side 1 and follows from it: “consequently” or “as a result”. Do not decide the logic from the topic. Decide it from whether side 2 goes along with side 1 or pushes against it.

Trap 2: contrast inside a similarity.

The two species occupy similar habitats; ______ their hunting strategies differ.

Students pick “similarly” because the first clause says “similar”. But the clause after the blank is about a difference, so the category is contrast: “however”.

Tip. The transition describes how the part after it relates to what came before. Students get caught matching the word to the clause before the blank. Always ask: how does the upcoming clause relate to the previous one?

Five more traps

TrapWhat to remember
Choosing by toneA formal word is not a logical word. “Consequently” sounds impressive and is wrong without a cause.
Treating every new fact as a contrastNew information can simply add. Contrast needs a turn: an opposite, a limit, a difference or a surprise.
Same topic, so “therefore”Sharing a topic does not make a cause. The question is not “are these related?” but “how are they related?”
Ignoring the exact job“Similarly” compares, “specifically” narrows, “indeed” emphasizes. All continue, and they are not interchangeable.
Reading only the sentence with the blankRead enough before it to understand both ideas.

parts.title: Part 6 · More worked examples
parts.html:
Early electric cars had limited range. ______ modern electric vehicles can travel over 300 miles on a single charge.

Side 1: old electric cars had limited range. Side 2: modern ones go far. Opposite directions, and no causal link: range did not improve because early cars were limited.

ChoiceVerdict
A) Similarly,Both sentences are about range, but the directions are opposite.
B) However,Correct. Contrast.
C) Therefore,Invents a cause.
D) For example,Side 2 is not an example of side 1.
The soil in the region is rich in minerals. ______ farming there yields exceptional harvests.

Side 1: rich soil. Side 2: great harvests. Side 2 is a consequence of side 1, since the soil explains the harvests. Category: result. “Therefore,” “Consequently,” or “As a result,”. “However” would claim the harvests happen despite the rich soil, which reverses the logic.

parts.title: Part 7 · Top tips
parts.html:
• Be flexible. There are many transitions, and the exact word you predicted may not be offered. Look for a choice with the same job: if you wanted “however” and it is missing, “on the other hand” or “though” may be there.
  • Eliminate copycats. If two choices do the same job (“also” and “in addition”, or “however” and “nevertheless”), they cannot both be right, so both are almost certainly wrong. They do not need to be exact synonyms, only the same kind of transition. Check the fine differences in the table in Part 2 before crossing out two contrast words.
  • Plug and play. Transition choices are short. When you are down to two, read the passage with each one and keep the one that gives the clearer meaning.

parts.title: Part 8 · Where the transition sits
parts.html:
In the middle or at the end, it still points backwards. A transition does not have to open its sentence. All three sentences below mean the same thing, and in all three “however” links the sentence to the one before it.

Desert foxes have very large ears.
However, arctic foxes have small ones.
Arctic foxes, however, have small ones.
Arctic foxes have small ones, however.

So when the blank sits between two commas in the middle of a sentence, do not try to relate the two halves of that sentence. “Arctic foxes” and “have small ones” have no relationship to find. Cross the blank out, read the sentence whole, and compare it with the previous sentence.

The exception: one comma. When the blank follows a single comma and joins two clauses that each have a subject and a verb, it links the two halves of its own sentence. The choices will be small joining words: so, but, for, whereas, while.

Arctic foxes have small ears and thick fur, ______ they lose very little heat. Two clauses in one sentence → the second is a result of the first → so

As a joining word, for means “because”, so it runs the other way: “They lose very little heat, for they have small ears and thick fur.”

parts.title: Part 9 · Transitions that are easy to misread
parts.html:
TransitionMeansExample
as suchbeing that kind of thing (it stands for a noun just used)Bats are mammals. As such, they feed their young on milk.
accordinglyso, in a way that fits what was just saidThe forecast warned of ice. Accordingly, the race was shortened.
to this endin order to achieve the goal just statedThe city wants cleaner air. To this end, it has banned older trucks.
that isin other words; often after a dashThe species is nocturnal—that is, active at night.
meanwhileat the same time; often marks a contrastSales of print books fell. Meanwhile, audiobook sales doubled.
subsequentlyafterwards (time only, not cause)The bridge opened in 1932. Subsequently, traffic tripled.
alternativelyas another optionThe samples can be frozen. Alternatively, they can be dried.
regardless, in any casewhatever the truth of the previous pointThe cause is still debated. Regardless, the damage is real.
likewisein the same wayWolves hunt in packs. Likewise, orcas hunt in groups.
indeed, in factstronger support for the point just madeThe tree is old. In fact, it is the oldest in the country.

Two to watch. “As such” is not a loose “therefore”: it works only when the sentence before it has just said what the subject is. And “in fact” does not introduce a contrast; it pushes the previous statement further in the same direction.
